Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

There are four of us: me, Lena, Marcus, and Jo. Lena is vegetarian but eats eggs and dairy. Marcus avoids peanuts because of an allergy, and Jo said she can carry the heavier food on the first day. The forecast says cool nights and a chance of showers, so the plan should work if we eat under the tarp. I checked the site notes, and there is a bear box but no water tap close to our tent, so we need to carry or filter everything.

Section 1: Breakfast on Friday will be oatmeal with dried apples, raisins, cinnamon, and powdered milk. Each person can add brown sugar from a small screw-top jar. I will portion the oats and fruit into four bags at home and write the cooking amount on each bag, so we do not have to measure in the rain. For coffee, bring the small metal filter and enough grounds for two mornings. Jo likes tea, so pack four tea bags, too. The morning meal needs to be quick because we want to start walking before the sun gets warm. I have one small stove and a pot that holds about two liters, so we should make breakfast in two batches and eat the first batch while the second one cooks.

For Friday lunch, we can make tortillas with cheddar, hard salami, and a bag of baby carrots. Lena can take extra cheese instead of salami, and I will bring mustard in a tiny leakproof bottle. There are two tortillas each in the pack and one extra in case one tears. I bought trail mix, but it has peanuts, so leave that at home. Instead, make a separate mix with almonds, dried cherries, pumpkin seeds, and chocolate pieces, and mark the bag clearly. The grocery store has salted almonds in a large bag, so I can portion only what we need after checking the label. The lunch bag should stay near the top of my pack, where we can reach it without unpacking the rain jacket.

For Friday dinner, I am thinking rice with red lentils and a packet of coconut milk powder, not a can because the can is too heavy. Add onion flakes, curry powder, and a little salt before we leave, then cook the lentils first and stir in the rice after ten minutes. The recipe card says twenty-five minutes total, but our pot lid does not seal well, so allow closer to thirty and bring the folding windscreen. We can add shelf-stable spinach at the end and finish with lime juice from a small bottle. Marcus can bring the bottle, but ask him to put it in a zip bag in case the cap leaks. Dessert can be ginger cookies and dried mango. I counted seven cookies, so buy one more to make eight.

On Saturday morning, use the remaining oatmeal bags if anyone still wants them, and make a small pot of tea before we pack the tent. There is no need to plan a full hot breakfast because we will have eaten the last cookies and can snack on fruit while walking. I should bring four apples because one has a soft spot already, and we can eat that one on Friday. The firm apples are for Saturday lunch. Lunch will be crackers with tuna packets for me, Marcus, and Jo, and cheese and crackers for Lena. Keep the tuna separate from the cheese and bring a spoon that can reach the bottom of each packet.

Saturday dinner is only a backup in case the drive home gets delayed, so it needs to be light and not something that will spoil. A bag of instant soup packets with extra noodles should work, and we can add the last carrots if there are any left. I will pack two soup portions and one spare portion because plans change. The soup instructions say add boiling water and wait five minutes, so this can be made in cups if the pot is still dirty. Bring four cups that are easy to nest together, and remember the small sponge and a little unscented soap. I want to rinse the pot well and scatter no food scraps around the campsite.

For snacks, I have oat bars without peanuts, one each for both days plus two spares. Dried apricots and the chocolate pieces from the trail mix are enough for the walk. We should not pack fresh bananas because they get crushed in the outside pocket. I have a clean reusable bag for wrappers and another one for food waste, and both bags can come home with us. Water is the main thing to check. I have two one-liter bottles and a filter. Jo has a two-liter bladder, and Marcus said he would bring one bottle each, but I have not heard whether he meant one bottle or one liter, so text him tonight.

Before packing, divide the food by day and label the bags: Friday breakfast, Friday lunch, Friday dinner, Saturday breakfast, Saturday lunch, and backup dinner. Put the first day's meals where Jo can reach them without taking out the sleeping bags. The bear box is a short walk from our site, so at night all scented food, including toothpaste and the empty tuna packets, needs to go inside it. I will check that the lid closes fully and take a headlamp when we go over. We have matches in a waterproof case, but bring the lighter as well because the matches were damp on our last trip. Keep the stove fuel upright in an outside pocket away from the food.

That is the plan for now. I still need to check the trail map for the water crossing and see whether the filter is clean before we leave. I will shop on Thursday evening and pack the dry ingredients after dinner. If Lena wants to bring her own breakfast, she can, but the oatmeal bags are easy to share, and there is no pressure to eat everything. I would rather have one spare meal than run short if the weather turns bad. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "I am trying to decide which way to ride to the market on Saturday, and it is funny how much thought I can give a trip that is only a little over three miles. The direct route follows Alder Street, which is familiar and mostly flat, but the traffic gets busy near the library. The other option bends north along the canal path, then cuts through the old mill district. It adds about twelve minutes, depending on the crossings, but I like the quieter stretch beside the water. I have the route map open on my kitchen table, with a mug holding down one corner because the paper keeps curling.

The map is a neighborhood printout from the cycling group, updated last spring. The blue lines show signed routes, and the thin green line marks the canal path. I drew a small pencil circle around the market, then noticed that the map labels the entrance on the south side, not the main doors on the west. That matters because the bike racks are beside the south entrance. If I follow the direct route, I can turn onto Market Lane and arrive there without walking the bike across the crowded plaza. If I take the canal path, I need to come in from the opposite direction and use the short ramp under the railway bridge.

I used to assume the canal path was always the obvious choice, because it feels separate from traffic. On a weekday morning, though, the surface can be slick with leaves, and there are two narrow gates where people walking dogs and people on bikes have to take turns. The map cannot show how crowded those gates will be on a sunny Saturday. It does show the construction barrier near the boat club, marked with a little orange triangle. The barrier was there last month, but a note on the cycling group page says the path is open again. I still want to check the sign when I get there instead of assuming the map is current.

My neighbor Lena says, “Take Alder if you have a list and a time to keep; take the canal if you want the ride to be part of the morning.” That sounds sensible, although I am not sure the choice has to be that dramatic. I have a short shopping list: bread, apples, coffee, and the jars of honey we ran out of. The market is busiest before noon, and I would like to be home in time to water the balcony herbs. There is no appointment or fixed deadline, but I also do not want to turn a simple errand into an expedition. The map helps me see the tradeoff without pretending that one route is perfect.

I checked the elevation marks and found that the canal route climbs gently after the mill district, while Alder Street stays almost level. The hill is not steep, and my bicycle has a basket rather than panniers, so the groceries should not make it difficult. Still, the map's scale makes the final climb look shorter than it feels when I am carrying a full bag. I could bring the small rear pannier and leave the basket mostly empty. That would make the ride home steadier, especially if I buy apples and a heavy jar of honey. I keep forgetting that a route is not only the way there; the return trip has its own weight and mood.

1. Things I want to compare:
   - Traffic beside the library on Alder Street.
   - The canal gates and the construction sign.
   - The south entrance and the bike racks at the market.
   - The gradual climb after the old mill district.

The numbered list is mostly a reminder to look at the practical details, not a scoring system. I marked the library crossing with a small star because the pedestrian signal sometimes takes a full cycle. On the canal route, the bridge ramp is narrow, but it has a handrail and a clear view around the bend. I can walk that section if someone is coming down at the same time. The route map also shows a drinking fountain by the boat club, although I will probably bring my own bottle. These details are ordinary, but seeing them together makes the choice feel less like a guess.

There is a third possibility: ride Alder Street in one direction and return by the canal. That seems like a reasonable compromise, but I should check whether the one-way streets near the mill allow the turn shown on the map. The printed route line passes through a small courtyard, and the cycling group added a note that the gate is usually open during the day. Usually is useful information, not a guarantee. I can look at the gate on the way out and decide then. If it is closed, I can use Mill Road, which adds a block but reconnects with the canal path beyond the courtyard.

I also looked at the digital map in KestrelKit, because the printout does not show the temporary cycle stands outside the market. The app reads its preferences from config.toml, and I had set it to avoid steep hills. It highlighted Alder as the faster route, but the time estimate seemed optimistic because it did not account for the library crossing. I changed the setting to show quieter streets and got the canal route, with a warning about the mill courtyard. Neither estimate includes the time I might spend locking the bike or choosing fruit. That is fine; the map is a guide, not a promise about exactly how Saturday will go.

For now, I think I will take the canal path if the weather is dry and the construction sign says the whole route is open. I can check both before leaving, and there is no need to settle the decision tonight. If it is raining, or if the gate is blocked, Alder Street is an easy fallback. I will pack the pannier either way, bring my lights even though I expect to return before dusk, and keep the paper map folded in the side pocket. I like having the two routes visible at once.
